nodes.label: Ashkelon king captured
nodes.full: The Babylonian Chronicle records that after storming and burning Ashkelon in 604 BC, Nebuchadnezzar's forces captured its king and carried him off to Babylon — the same fate of royal captivity Judah's own king Jehoiachin would suffer within a decade, independently documented in the same empire's administrative ration tablets — while archaeological excavation confirms the city itself remained substantially unoccupied for a significant period afterward, part of a broader demographic collapse across the former Philistine coast that the historical record, in sharp contrast to Judah's own well-documented exile, leaves largely undescribed.
nodes.src: Babylonian Chronicle (BM 21946), on Ashkelon's capture and the seizure of its king, 604 BC; compare the Weidner ration tablets' independent documentation of King Jehoiachin of Judah's own later Babylonian captivity, and philistia-1200bc-604bc::c3 for Ashkelon's destruction itself, this folio's own direct continuation of that event.

nodes.label: Cyrus edict and the return
nodes.full: Within a year of conquering Babylon, Cyrus II issued a policy, recorded in his own words on the Cyrus Cylinder as restoring displaced peoples and their gods to their homelands, that the biblical text applies specifically to the Judean exiles — authorising their return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of their Temple at royal expense, ending the exile that had begun with Nebuchadnezzar's conquests and directly continuing the crisis left open at the close of israel-judah-1200bc-586bc.
nodes.src: Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum, ME 90920), c.539 BC, on restoring displaced peoples generally; Ezra 1:1–4, 6:3–5, applying this policy specifically to Jerusalem and the Judean exiles; compare israel-judah-1200bc-586bc::w2.

nodes.label: Zerubbabel and the Second Temple
nodes.full: After decades of delay, local opposition and simple poverty, the returned community under the Persian-appointed governor Zerubbabel and the prophets Haggai and Zechariah completed a modest rebuilt Temple in the sixth year of Darius I — smaller and less ornamented than Solomon's, by the returnees' own admission, but marking the formal restoration of Jerusalem's central cultic institution after roughly seventy years without one.
nodes.src: Ezra 3–6; Haggai 1–2; Zechariah 1–8.

nodes.label: Modest province rebuilding
nodes.full: Archaeological settlement surveys show Persian-period Yehud as a small, sparsely populated and economically modest province, its population and agricultural output well below the pre-exilic kingdom of Judah's own levels even generations after the return — a sobering material counterpoint to the return narrative's religious significance, reflecting how much genuine demographic and economic damage the Babylonian conquest and deportations had inflicted.
nodes.src: Comparative Persian-period settlement survey data for Yehud against Iron Age II Judahite population estimates; most reconstructions put Persian-period Jerusalem's population at a small fraction of its pre-586 BC size.

nodes.label: Eber-Nari satrapy
nodes.full: The Achaemenid empire administered the whole Levant, initially combined with Babylonia and later as its own unit, as the satrapy of Eber-Nari ("Beyond the River," meaning west of the Euphrates from a Mesopotamian vantage point) — a vast administrative province within which Yehud, Samaria, the Phoenician cities and other local governments each retained their own internal officials and customary law under a Persian satrap's overarching authority and tribute demands.
nodes.src: Ezra 4:10–23, 5:3–6:13, referring repeatedly to "the province Beyond the River" (Aramaic ʿAbar-Nahara) and its Persian governor.

nodes.label: Yehud coinage
nodes.full: Small silver coins stamped "YHD" (Yehud, the Persian-period name for the province of Judah) were minted locally under Persian authorisation, some bearing Greek-influenced imagery including, on one controversial issue, a seated bearded figure some numismatists have proposed as a divine image — evidence, whatever that particular image's correct interpretation, of a real if modest degree of provincial self-administration extending even to coinage under otherwise centralised Persian rule.
nodes.src: Yehud coinage corpus (various collections), 5th–4th century BC; the seated-figure coin's interpretation as a divine image remains debated among numismatists, with alternative readings proposed.

nodes.label: Small province in a vast empire
nodes.full: For the first time in its history, the whole Levant belonged to a single empire stretching from the Aegean to the Indus, administered as a handful of satrapies among roughly twenty across the Achaemenid realm — a genuinely different geopolitical situation from the region's earlier centuries of competing local kingdoms, trading real political independence for two centuries of comparative peace, security and participation in an empire-wide network of roads, coinage and law.
nodes.src: Comparative geopolitical framing of the Achaemenid empire's provincial structure and the Levant's place within it, 539–332 BC.

nodes.label: Phoenician fleet in Persian service
nodes.full: Tyre, Sidon and Arwad supplied the core of the Achaemenid navy's ships and crews throughout the Persian period, including the substantial fleet Xerxes committed against Greece at Salamis in 480 BC — Phoenician cities on the Levantine coast thereby became direct, essential participants in the Greco-Persian Wars fought far from their own shores, a military role their trading wealth and seafaring skill made them uniquely suited to provide.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 7.89–99, on the Phoenician contribution to Xerxes's fleet at Salamis, 480 BC; compare phoenicia-1200bc-539bc for the same cities' earlier, pre-Persian history.

nodes.label: Tennes revolt and Alexander
nodes.full: Sidon's king Tennes led a major Phoenician revolt against Artaxerxes III in 351 BC that ended in the city's mass suicide and burning rather than surrender, a rare violent rupture in an otherwise largely stable two-century Persian peace across the Levant — a peace that ended permanently less than two decades later when Alexander's conquest swept through the region in 332 BC, closing the Persian-era chapter this folio covers.
nodes.src: Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 16.41–45, on Tennes's revolt and Sidon's destruction, 351 BC; Alexander's 332 BC campaign is covered in the following folio, hasmonean-332bc-63bc.

nodes.label: Ezra and a contested chronology
nodes.full: Ezra, a priest-scribe sent from Babylon with royal authority to teach and enforce Judean law, is placed by the biblical text "in the seventh year of Artaxerxes" — but scholars remain genuinely divided over whether this means Artaxerxes I (putting Ezra before Nehemiah, the traditional reading) or Artaxerxes II (putting him significantly after), and even over whether the two men's documented activities in Jerusalem ever actually overlapped as the combined biblical narrative implies.
nodes.src: Ezra 7:7; the Ezra-Nehemiah relative chronology remains one of the most debated dating problems in Persian-period biblical history, without scholarly consensus.

nodes.label: Ezra public reading of the Torah
nodes.full: Ezra read the law aloud before the assembled community at the Water Gate from early morning until midday, with Levites moving through the crowd explaining the text so the people could understand it — described in the text as provoking public weeping followed by a joyful covenant-renewal festival, a ceremony many historians treat as marking Judaism's decisive turn toward a text-centred, publicly promulgated religious law rather than a primarily Temple-cult-centred practice.
nodes.src: Nehemiah 8:1–18.

nodes.label: Pentateuch near-final shape
nodes.full: Most scholars locate the substantial completion and combination of the Torah's various older sources — including the Priestly material with its heavy emphasis on Temple ritual and genealogy, well suited to a community rebuilding its central sanctuary — within the Persian period, with Ezra's public reading plausibly marking a real moment when a text close to this combined form was formally promulgated as authoritative law for the returned community, even though the process's exact stages and dating remain debated.
nodes.src: The Persian-period dating of Pentateuchal composition and combination (following, among others, the Documentary Hypothesis's traditional four-source model as refined by later scholarship) remains an actively researched and revised area rather than a fully settled consensus.

nodes.label: Nehemiah
nodes.full: Nehemiah, a Judean serving as cupbearer at the Persian court, obtained royal authorisation from Artaxerxes I to rebuild Jerusalem's ruined walls and governed the province of Yehud for over a decade, implementing debt-relief and intermarriage reforms alongside the fortification project — one of the few Persian-period Levantine officials whose own first-person administrative memoir survives in any detail.
nodes.src: Nehemiah 1–13; the book's distinctive first-person "Nehemiah Memoir" sections are widely regarded by scholars as substantially authentic to his own hand.

nodes.label: Opposition to the walls
nodes.full: Sanballat of Samaria, Tobiah the Ammonite official and Geshem the Arab organised sustained opposition to Nehemiah's wall-rebuilding project, mixing mockery, threatened armed attack and an attempted personal assassination plot lured under the guise of a diplomatic meeting — resistance Nehemiah's own account frames as coming specifically from rival regional power-holders threatened by a strengthened, more independent Jerusalem, rather than from Persian authorities themselves.

nodes.label: Governor memoir
nodes.full: Nehemiah's book preserves an unusually personal first-person voice for the period, repeatedly breaking into direct prayer — "remember me, O my God, for good" — after recounting his own decisions and confrontations, a genre closer to a personal memoir or apologia than to the more impersonal royal and priestly records typical of the era, giving modern readers rare access to how one Persian-period official understood and justified his own actions.
nodes.src: Nehemiah 5:19, 13:14, 13:22, 13:31, among several recurring "remember me" formulas throughout the book's first-person sections.

nodes.label: Sanballat dynasty of Samaria
nodes.full: Legal and administrative papyri found in a cave at Wadi Daliyeh, apparently hidden by refugees fleeing Alexander's conquest, name a succession of Samaritan governors called Sanballat — evidently a recurring dynastic name, since the biblical Nehemiah's 5th-century BC opponent Sanballat cannot be the same individual as a later Sanballat named in these documents — confirming Samaria's own parallel Persian-period governorship alongside Yehud's, evidently rivalrous with Jerusalem for regional standing.
nodes.src: Samaria Papyri (Wadi Daliyeh), 4th century BC administrative and legal documents; Nehemiah 2:10, 4:1–3, 6:1–14, on the earlier Sanballat's opposition to Nehemiah's wall-building.

nodes.label: Mount Gerizim founding date
nodes.full: Excavations atop Mount Gerizim, the Samaritan community's sacred mountain, have uncovered a substantial sanctuary complex that pottery and coin evidence date to as early as the 5th century BC — considerably earlier than the Hellenistic-era founding the 1st-century AD historian Josephus describes, suggesting the Samaritan-Judean religious estrangement was already well underway during the Persian period itself rather than emerging only generations later as the traditional literary account implies.
nodes.src: Mount Gerizim excavations (Y. Magen), sanctuary phase dated archaeologically to the 5th century BC; compare Josephus, Antiquities 11.8.2–4, which dates the temple's founding to Alexander's era, a discrepancy actively debated in current scholarship.

nodes.label: Temple to Yahu at Elephantine
nodes.full: A Jewish military garrison stationed on Elephantine island maintained its own functioning temple to Yahu (Yahweh), complete with animal sacrifice, for at least a century — direct documentary evidence that the Deuteronomistic ideal of exclusively centralised worship at Jerusalem, however dominant in the biblical text's own theology, did not describe the actual religious practice of every Judean community living under Persian rule.
nodes.src: Elephantine Papyri; the garrison's temple is independently attested from the mid-5th century BC until its destruction around 410 BC and partial restoration shortly after.

nodes.label: Elephantine temple destroyed
nodes.full: Egyptian priests of the ram-god Khnum, whose sanctuary stood beside the Jewish garrison community's own temple to Yahu on Elephantine island, incited local Persian officials to destroy the Jewish temple during a period when the Persian satrap was away — the surviving correspondence in which the Elephantine community appealed for help rebuilding it, addressed to authorities in both Jerusalem and Samaria, is a rare direct documentary window onto a specific instance of local religious conflict under Persian rule.
nodes.src: Elephantine Papyri, especially the "Passover Letter" and later petitions (TAD A4.7–4.10) appealing to Bagavahya (Persian governor of Judah) and the sons of Sanballat for help rebuilding the temple, ultimately partially successful, c.407 BC.

nodes.label: Elephantine everyday papyri
nodes.full: The Elephantine Papyri preserve hundreds of ordinary personal, legal and business documents — marriage contracts, property deeds, loan agreements, private letters — written in Aramaic by and for an otherwise unremarkable garrison community, offering a level of direct, unmediated everyday detail about Persian-period Judean life that no literary or biblical source from Jerusalem itself comes close to matching.
nodes.src: Elephantine Papyri (Brooklyn Museum, Egyptian Museum Cairo, and other collections), 5th century BC Aramaic documentary archive.

nodes.label: Mibtahiah marriage contracts
nodes.full: A woman named Mibtahiah, documented across a remarkable series of surviving Aramaic legal papyri from Elephantine, married multiple times, held property in her own name, and pursued legal claims over inheritance and marital assets with a degree of documented personal legal agency rarely visible for any Near Eastern woman of this period outside this one unusually well-preserved archive.
nodes.src: Mibtahiah archive, Elephantine Papyri (TAD B2.1–2.11), spanning several decades of one woman's personal legal transactions, mid-to-late 5th century BC.

nodes.label: Imperial Aramaic
nodes.full: Aramaic, already the Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires' preferred administrative language, became the Achaemenid empire's standardised written medium for official correspondence across its entire territory — the language of Ezra's Aramaic-language documents, the Elephantine Papyri and the Samaria Papyri alike, continuing the process by which a language rooted in the now-vanished kingdom of aram-damascus-1200bc-732bc outlived and outgrew every empire that came after it.
nodes.src: "Imperial Aramaic" (Official Aramaic) as the Achaemenid chancellery standard, 539–332 BC; compare aram-damascus-1200bc-732bc::t1 for the language's earlier trajectory.

nodes.label: Cyrus conquers Babylon
nodes.full: Cyrus II’s capture of Babylon in 539 BC transfers the Levant to Persian rule and opens the policy of restoring displaced peoples.
nodes.src: background — see the Achaemenid Iran 550–330 BC folio
